statement: Eight people sit around a round table. Each is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies. Every one of them says: 'Both of my neighbours are knaves.' What is the smallest possible number of knights at the table?

choices.misconception: I thought a table of knaves works because liars can say anything, but then every statement would be true.
I thought one knight with knaves all round was enough, but a knave far from the knight would be telling the truth.
I placed a knight in every fourth seat, missing that the knave halfway between two knights has two knave neighbours.
I assumed knights and knaves must alternate around the table.

hints: What must be true about the neighbours of a knave?
A knight’s statement is true, so knights are never next to each other. A knave’s statement is false, so every knave sits next to a knight. Find the fewest knights meeting both conditions on 8 seats.
Each knight can 'cover' itself and its two neighbours, at most 3 seats. Covering 8 seats needs at least 3 knights.

solutions.reliable: A knight's neighbours are both knaves, so no two knights sit together. A knave is lying, so at least one neighbour of every knave is a knight. Each knight looks after at most 3 seats (itself and its two neighbours), so 2 knights cover at most 6 of the 8 seats and some knave would have two knave neighbours, making its statement true. With 3 knights in seats 1, 4 and 7 every condition holds: each knight has knave neighbours, and every knave sits beside a knight. So the smallest number is 3. The transferable idea: turn each statement into a condition on the seating, then find the extreme case and prove nothing smaller works.

whyOnTest: Knights and knaves puzzles reward converting statements into conditions; a minimum then needs both an example and a reason nothing smaller works.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
